```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 9,
                      fig.height = 7, out.width = "100%", dpi = 60)
join_and <- function(v) sub(", ([^,]*)$", " and \\1", toString(v))
n_steps <- length(unique(hypergraphs::tutoring_events$step))
```

Hypergraphs extend ordinary networks by allowing edges to connect more
than two nodes. These edges, called hyperedges, can represent interactions
or associations involving an entire group. Hyperedges can differ in size,
allowing pairs and larger groups to be represented within the same
hypergraph.

For example, consider a scientific article written by three researchers.
A coauthorship network represents the article by connecting each pair of
authors, producing three edges. A hypergraph represents the article by one
hyperedge containing all three authors. An article with four authors forms
a hyperedge containing four nodes. Each hyperedge therefore identifies
the complete authorship group associated with an article.

This tutorial uses an event log from an AI tutoring system. Event types
are nodes, and each trial forms a hyperedge containing the distinct event
types recorded within it. The analysis examines which events occur
together within trials, how frequently they participate, and how they form
communities. The examples introduce hypergraph construction, structural
measures, centrality, clustering, and comparison with randomised
hypergraphs using the `hypergraphs` R package.

## Data

The examples use `tutoring_events`, an event log containing
`r format(n_steps, big.mark = ",")` problem steps completed or discontinued
by learners working with an AI tutor. Each row records one event. A step
begins with a task and can include an initial answer, tutor feedback, and
further attempts. The events `Completed` and `Stopped` identify the recorded
outcomes. A trial is one attempt and its associated events within a step;
the supplied `trial` identifier defines its boundaries.

```{r data}
library(hypergraphs)
head(tutoring_events, 12)
```

```{r data-values, include = FALSE}
n_trials <- length(unique(tutoring_events$trial))
n_events <- length(unique(tutoring_events$event))
```

There are `r format(n_trials, big.mark = ",")` trials and
`r n_events` event types. The event types, rather than individual event
occurrences, will be the nodes of the hypergraph.

## Hypergraphs from observed groups

Begin by specifying the observational unit. Here, each trial is an
observed group, and its distinct event types form a hyperedge. In
`hypergraph()`, `action = "event"` identifies the event-type column and
`session = "trial"` identifies the grouping column. The resulting object
retains one hyperedge per trial, including trials with identical membership.
This representation records which event types occurred together; it does
not retain their order or repeated occurrences within a trial.

```{r trials}
trial_hg <- hypergraph(tutoring_events, action = "event", session = "trial")
trial_hg
```

```{r trials-values, include = FALSE}
trial_edges <- hg_get(trial_hg)
size_counts <- table(trial_edges$size)
modal_size <- names(size_counts)[which.max(size_counts)]
n_sets <- length(unique(trial_edges$members))
```

The most common hyperedge size is `r modal_size` distinct event types,
and the largest is `r max(trial_edges$size)`. The
`r format(n_trials, big.mark = ",")` trials contain `r n_sets` distinct
member sets. The argument `top` controls how many sets are displayed:
a whole number, such as `top = 4`, selects that many most frequent sets;
a fraction, such as `top = 0.95`, selects the most frequent sets whose
cumulative counts cover at least 95% of trials. The set that crosses the
threshold is included in full, so coverage can exceed the requested share.
Use `top = Inf` to retain every set. The object `trial_hg` retains every
trial for the subsequent analyses.

```{r trials-plot, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 9, fig.alt = "The most frequent event sets covering at least 95 percent of trials, with shared events appearing in overlapping regions"}
trial_preview <- hypergraph(tutoring_events, action = "event",
                            session = "trial", top = 0.95)
plot(trial_preview) +
  ggplot2::guides(size = ggplot2::guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

The `r nrow(hg_get(trial_preview, what = "sets"))` retained sets account for
`r round(100 * sum(hg_get(trial_preview, what = "sets")$share), 2)`% of trials.
Each enclosed region contains the event types in one set, and overlapping
regions indicate shared event types. Colour indicates set frequency, and
node size summarises event participation.

A minimum support threshold selects sets by their individual frequencies.
Here, support is the proportion of trials with exactly the same event set.
With `min_share = 0.01`, a set is retained when it accounts for at least
1% of trials.

```{r common-trials}
common_trials <- hypergraph(tutoring_events, action = "event",
                            session = "trial", min_share = 0.01)
common_trials
```

```{r common-trials-values, include = FALSE}
common_cover <- round(100 * sum(hg_get(common_trials, what = "sets")$share))
```

```{r common-trials-plot, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 9}
plot(common_trials)
```

The `r nrow(hg_get(common_trials))` retained sets account for
`r common_cover`% of trials. The set containing `Comfort`, `GiveUp`, and
`Stopped` describes a recorded termination pattern. Its position in the
figure summarises shared membership; distances between plotted regions are
not estimates of differences in learning outcomes.

Read the node table with `hg_get()`. In this trial-level representation,
the degree of an event type is the number of trials containing it.

```{r trial-nodes}
trial_nodes <- hg_get(trial_hg, what = "nodes", sort_by = "degree")
trial_nodes
```

## Frequent sets

An alternative summary retains a fixed number of frequent event sets.
The following call selects the eight sets with the largest counts. This
changes the unit represented by a hyperedge from an individual trial to a
distinct event set, with its frequency stored as an attribute.

```{r sets}
trial_sets <- hypergraph(tutoring_events, action = "event",
                         session = "trial", top = 8)
trial_set_table <- hg_get(trial_sets, what = "sets")
trial_set_table
```

```{r sets-values, include = FALSE}
top_share <- round(100 * sum(trial_set_table$share))
most_frequent_set <- hg_get(trial_sets, what = "sets", top = 1)$set
```

These eight sets account for `r top_share`% of trials. The most frequent
set is `r most_frequent_set`, which contains the events associated with a
correct initial response. Other retained sets include incorrect responses
and reattempts following tutor feedback. These labels describe co-occurrence
within trials; the event order must be examined in the original log.

```{r sets-plot, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 7}
plot(trial_sets)
```

To compare outcomes, count sets separately within each value of
`outcome`. The argument `group = "outcome"` performs this comparison, and
`top = 6` retains the six most frequent sets in each group. The outcome is
defined for the complete problem step, so trials preceding its termination
are grouped by that final outcome.

```{r sets-by}
outcome_sets <- hypergraph(tutoring_events, action = "event",
                         session = "trial", group = "outcome", top = 6)
outcome_set_table <- hg_get(outcome_sets, what = "sets")
outcome_set_table
```

```{r sets-completed-plot, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 7}
plot(outcome_sets, group = "completed")
```

```{r sets-stopped-plot, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 7}
plot(outcome_sets, group = "stopped")
```

Compare the two tables and plots to identify event combinations that
are frequent within completed and stopped steps. The set
`Comfort + GiveUp + Stopped`, for example, occurs in stopped steps and
contains a tutor response, learner withdrawal, and termination. Differences
between the groups are descriptive associations. They do not establish an
effect of a particular tutor response on completion.

## Hypergraphs from sequences

A window-based representation uses local sequence positions as its
observational units. The following call forms overlapping windows of three
events within each problem step. `action` identifies event types, `actor`
identifies the independent sequences, and `time` specifies their ordering.
Each window contributes its distinct event types. Windows with identical
membership are combined, and their count is retained as a hyperedge weight.

```{r window}
window_hg <- hypergraph(tutoring_events, action = "event", actor = "step",
                        time = "position", window = 3)
window_hg
window_edges <- hg_get(window_hg, sort_by = "weight", top = 8)
window_edges
```

```{r window-plot, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 9}
plot(window_hg)
```

```{r window-values, include = FALSE}
n_windows <- sum(hg_get(window_hg)$weight)
```

The `r format(n_windows, big.mark = ",")` windows produce
`r nrow(hg_get(window_hg))` distinct member sets. A three-position window
can contain fewer than three event types when an event repeats. The next
example uses `min_weight = 2000` to retain recurrent sets and
`hg_subset(size = 3)` to select sets with three distinct event types.
Nodes without a retained membership are removed by the subset operation.

```{r window-frequent}
frequent_windows <- hypergraph(tutoring_events, action = "event",
                               actor = "step", time = "position",
                               window = 3, min_weight = 2000)
frequent_windows <- hg_subset(frequent_windows, size = 3)
frequent_windows
```

```{r window-frequent-plot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 7}
plot(frequent_windows)
```

The regions now represent recurring sets of three distinct events.
Window boundaries are determined by the chosen length and sequence unit.
Because the sequence unit is a problem step, a window can cross a trial
boundary within that step. The remaining sections use observed trials so
that their measures refer to the same grouping throughout.

## Projection to a network

The clique projection connects two event types when they occur in at
least one common trial. For the binary incidence used here, the projected
edge weight equals the number of shared trials. Weighted incidence has a
different interpretation, so the weighting convention should always be
specified when reporting a projection.

```{r project}
trial_network <- pairwise_network(trial_hg)
trial_network_edges <- hg_get(trial_network, sort_by = "weight", top = 8)
trial_network_edges
```

```{r project-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 7}
plot(trial_network)
```

```{r project-values-pre, include = FALSE}
n_pairs <- nrow(hg_get(trial_network))
```

Edge width increases with the number of trials containing both events.
The strong connections among `Task`, `Attempt`, `Correct`, and `Completed`
reflect their frequent joint occurrence. The projection summarises pairwise
counts, but it cannot identify which additional event types accompanied each
pair in a particular trial.

A network can also generate a hypergraph through its cliques. A clique
is a set of nodes in which every pair is connected. The next call promotes
cliques of three to six nodes to hyperedges. These are candidate groups
defined by pairwise connectivity; they need not correspond to observed
trials. `include_pairwise = FALSE` excludes size-two hyperedges.

```{r project-back}
clique_hg <- hypergraph(trial_network, max_size = 6, include_pairwise = FALSE)
clique_hg
```

```{r project-back-plot, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 8}
plot(clique_hg)
```

```{r project-values, include = FALSE}
as_keys <- function(members) {
  vapply(strsplit(members, ", ", fixed = TRUE),
         \(m) paste(sort(m), collapse = " + "), character(1))
}
observed_keys <- as_keys(unique(hg_get(trial_hg)$members))
observed_keys <- observed_keys[lengths(strsplit(observed_keys, " + ",
                                                fixed = TRUE)) >= 3]
inferred_keys <- as_keys(hg_get(clique_hg)$members)
n_true <- sum(inferred_keys %in% observed_keys)
n_found <- sum(observed_keys %in% inferred_keys)
```

The projected network has `r n_pairs` connected pairs and
`r nrow(hg_get(clique_hg))` cliques of sizes three to
`r max(hg_get(clique_hg)$size)`. The trial data contain
`r length(observed_keys)` distinct sets of at least three event types, of
which `r n_found` are recovered among these cliques. A further
`r nrow(hg_get(clique_hg)) - n_true` cliques have no matching observed set.
A clique without an exact observed match can be contained in a larger
observed set or can combine pairwise connections from different trials.
Pairwise connectivity therefore does not establish that a clique occurred
as a complete trial event set. The dense overlap of regions also limits the value
of this plot as a display of individual cliques.

## Node measures

The incidence matrix has one row per event type and one column per
trial. A cell is one when the event type occurs in the trial and zero
otherwise. From this matrix, `hg_measures()` reports the hyperdegree
(number of incident trials), strength (sum of the sizes of incident trials),
and number of neighbours (distinct other event types sharing a trial).
The strength definition is specific to this structural summary and should
not be confused with event frequency.

```{r measures}
node_measures <- hg_measures(trial_hg)
node_measures
trial_summary <- hg_measures(trial_hg, what = "summary")
trial_summary
```

```{r measures-values, include = FALSE}
participation <- subset(trial_summary,
                        measure == "pairwise_participation")$value
attempt_row <- subset(node_measures, node == "Attempt")
```

`Attempt` occurs in `r format(attempt_row$hyperdegree, big.mark = ",")`
trials and shares those trials with `r attempt_row$n_neighbors` other event
types. Hyperdegree measures participation across trials, whereas neighbour
count measures the range of co-occurring events. Pairwise participation is
the proportion of all event-type pairs observed together at least once.
Its value is `r sprintf("%.2f", participation)`, meaning that
`r round(100 * (1 - participation))`% of possible pairs never share a trial.

## Centrality

Clique-motif eigenvector centrality assigns larger scores to event
types connected to other high-scoring event types. It is computed from
the binary-membership clique projection, whose weights count shared
hyperedges (Benson 2019). Use `sort_by = "clique"` to inspect the ranking.

```{r centrality}
event_centrality <- hg_centrality(trial_hg, sort_by = "clique")
event_centrality
```

The high-ranking event types include `Task`, `Attempt`, `Correct`, and
`Completed`. Their scores reflect both frequent participation and their
connections to other high-scoring events. Centrality describes structural
position in this representation; it is not a measure of instructional
effectiveness.

Benson's (2019) Z and H centralities use products of the scores of
other members of a hyperedge. Their definitions require a uniform
hypergraph, with a common size for all non-singleton hyperedges. The trial
hypergraph has mixed sizes, so these two methods cannot be applied to it
directly. Clique centrality and PageRank accept mixed hyperedge sizes.

Hypergraph PageRank describes a random walk with two stages: choose
an incident hyperedge, then choose a node within it. Edge and incidence
weights determine these probabilities. With the default damping factor of
0.85, the walker follows this transition with probability 0.85 and restarts
uniformly with probability 0.15. The stationary probabilities form a ranking
of the nodes (Chitra and Raphael 2019).

```{r pagerank}
event_pagerank <- hg_pagerank(trial_hg, sort_by = "pagerank")
event_pagerank
```

Compare the PageRank and clique rankings for `Comfort`, `GiveUp`, and
`Stopped`. Their close co-occurrence creates a small region in which the
random walk can remain for several transitions. PageRank and clique
centrality weight this structure differently, so agreement between their
rankings should be examined rather than assumed.

## Communities and clusters

Community detection partitions nodes according to an optimisation
criterion. The default `hg_communities()` applies Infomap to the association
projection and minimises the description length of a random walk. The
following call uses 20 seeds and reports the medoid partition: the run with
the greatest total adjusted mutual information with the other runs.
This selects a representative result from the ensemble.

```{r communities, eval = requireNamespace("igraph", quietly = TRUE)}
event_communities <- hg_communities(trial_hg, n_runs = 20, seeds = 1:20)
event_communities
```

Spectral clustering instead embeds nodes in eigenvectors of the
normalised hypergraph Laplacian and partitions the embedding by k-means.
The analyst specifies `k`, here three clusters. The seed makes the random
initialisation of k-means reproducible; it does not establish that three
clusters are the appropriate resolution.

```{r cluster}
event_clusters <- hg_cluster(trial_hg, k = 3, seed = 1)
event_clusters
```

```{r cluster-values, include = FALSE}
members_of <- function(event) {
  label <- subset(event_clusters, node == event)$cluster
  join_and(subset(event_clusters, cluster == label)$node)
}
```

The three clusters group the events associated with termination
(`r members_of("Stopped")`), completion (`r members_of("Completed")`), and
tutor feedback or reattempts (`r members_of("Guidance")`). Compare these
groups with the Infomap partition using the adjusted Rand index. This
index equals one for identical partitions and has an expected value near
zero under its chance model; it can also be negative.

```{r agreement, eval = requireNamespace("igraph", quietly = TRUE)}
partition_agreement <- hg_agreement(event_communities, event_clusters)
partition_agreement
partition_table <- hg_agreement(event_communities, event_clusters,
                                what = "table")
partition_table
```

```{r agreement-text, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = requireNamespace("igraph", quietly = TRUE)}
cat(sprintf(paste(
  "The adjusted Rand index between the two fitted partitions is %.2f.",
  "Use the cross-tabulation to identify event groups that remain together",
  "or are divided differently under the two objectives."),
  partition_agreement$ari))
```

## Null models

To assess a structural statistic, specify a reference distribution.
The swap null model used here preserves each node's hyperdegree and each
hyperedge's size while changing their memberships. It generates successive
randomised incidence matrices through checkerboard swaps. The example
uses trials from stopped steps and compares their pairwise participation,
mean Jaccard overlap, and number of repeated event sets with this null
distribution.

```{r null}
stopped_events <- subset(tutoring_events, outcome == "stopped")
stopped_hg <- hypergraph(stopped_events, action = "event", session = "trial")
plot(stopped_hg)
stopped_null <- hg_null_test(stopped_hg, n = 19, seed = 1,
                          statistic = c("pairwise_participation",
                                        "avg_jaccard", "repeated_edges"))
stopped_null
```

```{r null-values, include = FALSE}
null_row <- function(s) subset(stopped_null, statistic == s)
pp <- null_row("pairwise_participation")
re <- null_row("repeated_edges")
aj <- null_row("avg_jaccard")
```

Observed pairwise participation is `r round(100 * pp$observed)`%,
compared with a null mean of `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * pp$null_mean)`%.
There are `r format(re$observed, big.mark = ",")` repeated trial sets,
compared with a null mean of
`r format(round(re$null_mean), big.mark = ",")`. Mean Jaccard overlap is
`r round(aj$observed, 2)` in the data and `r round(aj$null_mean, 2)` under
the null. These comparisons quantify structure beyond the preserved
degrees and hyperedge sizes. They remain conditional on this particular
randomisation model.

Only 19 draws are used to keep this example short. The smallest attainable
Monte Carlo p-value is 1/20 = 0.05; the reported value for pairwise
participation is `r pp$p_value`. A larger number of draws, such as 999 or
more, is needed to estimate smaller tail probabilities. The standardised
deviations are `r round(pp$z, 1)` for pairwise participation and
`r round(re$z, 1)` for repeated sets. These z-scores summarise distance
from the null mean and do not assume that the null distribution is normal.

## Other higher-order structures

The package also supports related representations. `text_hypergraph()`
constructs relations between documents and words. `hon()` estimates memory
networks in which transition probabilities can depend on previous states.
`simplicial()` constructs complexes that include every subset of each
simplex. These representations encode different assumptions about the
observations. See `?hypergraphs` for their definitions and entry points.

https://doi.org/10.1137/18M1203031

Chitra, U., & Raphael, B. J. (2019). Random walks on hypergraphs with
edge-dependent vertex weights. *Proceedings of ICML*, PMLR 97, 1172–1181.
https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/chitra19a.html

Hayashi, K., Aksoy, S. G., Park, C. H., & Park, H. (2020). Hypergraph random
walks, Laplacians, and clustering. *Proceedings of CIKM*, 495–504.
https://doi.org/10.1145/3340531.3412034

Zhou, D., Huang, J., & Schölkopf, B. (2006). Learning with hypergraphs:
Clustering, classification, and embedding. *Advances in Neural Information
Processing Systems*, 19, 1601–1608.
